subject: biology
title: Animal body plans
summary: How animals are classified by symmetry, germ layers, body cavities and developmental patterns, an overview of the major phyla, and how life history traits vary among animals.
body:
There are well over a million described animal species, but most of them are built on a small number of basic body plans. A **body plan** is the set of structural and developmental features shared by a group of animals: their symmetry, tissue layers, body cavity and the way the embryo develops. Learning these features lets you make sense of animal diversity, read a phylogenetic tree and predict a great deal about an unfamiliar animal from a few observations.

## Think of it like this

### Radial and bilateral symmetry are like a pizza and a car

A round pizza can be cut through the centre in many directions and each cut gives two matching halves, which is **radial symmetry**. A jellyfish or sea anemone is built like that pizza: it drifts or sits still and meets food and danger equally from every side. A car is different: only one cut, straight down the middle from front to back, gives mirror halves, which is **bilateral symmetry**. Because a car always drives forwards, the headlights and sensors are packed at the front, just as animals that move in one direction concentrate their sense organs and nerve tissue at the **anterior** end (**cephalisation**).

*Where the analogy breaks down:* cars are designed, but body symmetry evolved; and sea stars show it can change, because adults are radial while their larvae are bilateral, revealing bilateral ancestors.

### A body cavity is like a water balloon

Squeeze a water balloon at one end and it gets longer and thinner; squeeze it around the middle and it bulges at the ends. Fluid can't be compressed, so it pushes back against whatever squeezes it. That is how a **hydrostatic skeleton** works: an earthworm's muscles contract against the fluid in its **coelom**, making each part of the body longer and thinner or shorter and fatter so it can burrow. The cavity also gives the gut and organs room to move and grow without being dragged around by the body wall.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* a balloon is one open bag, while an earthworm's coelom is lined by **mesoderm**-derived tissue and divided into segments, so each segment can change shape on its own.

### Life history trade-offs are like spending a weekly pay packet

If you earn a fixed amount from your part-time job, money spent on going out can't also go into savings. An organism's energy is the same: what goes into reproduction is not available for growth, maintenance or survival, which is a **trade-off**. **Semelparity** is like saving for years and blowing everything on one huge 18th birthday party, as the male antechinus does in one intense mating season before dying. **Iteroparity** is like spending a bit every week for years. Buying 50 cheap lolly bags versus one expensive present is like making many small offspring versus a few with lots of investment each.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* animals don't plan a budget; natural selection shapes which strategy works best, and a semelparous "one party" often produces a huge number of offspring, not few.

### In real life

At an Australian beach, the sting from a jellyfish or bluebottle comes from **cnidocytes**, the stinging cells that define phylum Cnidaria. Identical twins are possible in humans because, as **deuterostomes**, our early embryo cells have **indeterminate** cleavage, so a split early embryo can form two complete babies. Fishers and conservation managers use life history and survivorship data to judge how quickly a fish population could recover.

## Key ideas

### What makes an animal

Animals are multicellular, heterotrophic eukaryotes that ingest their food. Their cells lack cell walls and are held together by structural proteins, notably collagen. Most have nerve and muscle tissue, reproduce sexually with a dominant diploid stage, and go through an embryonic stage called the **blastula** (a hollow ball of cells) and then **gastrulation**, in which cells move inwards to form layers. Many animals share **Hox genes**, a family of regulatory genes that control the identity of body regions along the head-to-tail axis.

### Tissues and symmetry

Sponges (phylum Porifera) lack true tissues; their cells are specialised but not organised into tissues separated by membranes. All other animals have true tissues and are called **eumetazoans**.

**Symmetry** describes how body parts are arranged around an axis:

- **Asymmetry** — no plane divides the body into matching halves (most sponges).
- **Radial symmetry** — body parts are arranged around a central axis, so many planes through the axis give mirror halves. It suits animals that are sessile or drift, meeting the environment equally from all sides (jellyfish, sea anemones).
- **Bilateral symmetry** — only one plane divides the body into left and right mirror halves. These animals have a dorsal (top) and ventral (bottom) side, an anterior (front) and posterior (rear) end. Bilateral symmetry is linked to directed movement and **cephalisation**, the concentration of sensory organs and nerve tissue at the anterior end, forming a head.

Adult echinoderms such as sea stars are radially (usually five-part) symmetrical, but their larvae are bilateral, which shows they descend from bilateral ancestors.

### Germ layers

During gastrulation, the embryo forms **germ layers**, which give rise to all the tissues and organs:

- **Ectoderm** (outer) — outer covering (epidermis) and the nervous system.
- **Endoderm** (inner) — lining of the digestive tract and associated organs such as the liver.
- **Mesoderm** (middle) — muscle, most organs between the gut and the outer covering, and in vertebrates the skeleton and blood.

**Diploblastic** animals have only ectoderm and endoderm (cnidarians such as jellyfish and corals). **Triploblastic** animals have all three layers; this includes all bilaterally symmetrical animals. Mesoderm made possible the development of complex muscles and organs.

### Body cavities

Many triploblastic animals have a **body cavity**, a fluid-filled space between the gut and the outer body wall. A body cavity cushions organs, allows the gut and organs to move and grow independently of the body wall, and can act as a **hydrostatic skeleton**, a fluid-filled support against which muscles contract.

- **Coelom** — a true body cavity, completely lined by tissue derived from mesoderm. Animals with one are **coelomates** (annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, chordates).
- **Pseudocoelom** — a cavity lined partly by mesoderm and partly by endoderm. Animals with one are **pseudocoelomates** (for example roundworms, phylum Nematoda).
- **Acoelomates** have no body cavity; the space between gut and wall is filled with tissue (flatworms, phylum Platyhelminthes).

Molecular phylogenies show that body cavity type does not neatly define evolutionary groups; coeloms seem to have been lost or reduced more than once. So body cavity is useful as a description of structure, but not on its own as evidence of relatedness.

### Protostomes and deuterostomes

Bilateral animals divide into two great lineages that differ in early development.

| Feature | Protostomes | Deuterostomes |
|---|---|---|
| Cleavage | Usually **spiral** and **determinate** (fate of each early cell fixed early) | Usually **radial** and **indeterminate** (early cells can each form a whole embryo) |
| Coelom formation | Splitting of solid masses of mesoderm (schizocoely) | Out-pocketing of the archenteron wall (enterocoely) |
| Fate of blastopore | Usually becomes the **mouth** | Usually becomes the **anus**; mouth forms later |
| Examples | Molluscs, annelids, arthropods, nematodes, flatworms | Echinoderms, chordates |

The **blastopore** is the opening into the primitive gut (archenteron) formed during gastrulation. The name protostome means "first mouth" and deuterostome "second mouth". Indeterminate cleavage is the reason identical twins can form in humans.

Modern phylogenies split protostomes into two clades. **Lophotrochozoa** includes flatworms, molluscs and annelids; many have a ciliated feeding structure (lophophore) or a trochophore larva. **Ecdysozoa** includes nematodes and arthropods, which grow by **ecdysis** (moulting a cuticle or exoskeleton).

### Overview of major phyla

| Phylum | Examples | Key features |
|---|---|---|
| Porifera | Sponges | No true tissues; choanocytes filter water; asymmetric |
| Cnidaria | Jellyfish, corals, anemones | Radial; diploblastic; stinging cells (cnidocytes); gastrovascular cavity with one opening |
| Platyhelminthes | Flatworms, tapeworms | Bilateral; acoelomate; flattened body; gut with one opening (absent in tapeworms) |
| Nematoda | Roundworms | Pseudocoelomate; cuticle moulted; complete gut |
| Annelida | Earthworms, leeches, marine worms | Segmented; coelomate; closed circulation |
| Mollusca | Snails, bivalves, octopus | Muscular foot, visceral mass, mantle; many with a shell |
| Arthropoda | Insects, crustaceans, spiders | Segmented; jointed appendages; chitin exoskeleton; moulting |
| Echinodermata | Sea stars, sea urchins | Deuterostome; adult radial symmetry; water vascular system; endoskeleton |
| Chordata | Sea squirts, fish, mammals | Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, post-anal tail at some stage |

Arthropods are by far the most species-rich phylum. Chordates include vertebrates, in which a backbone develops around the notochord.

### Life history traits

A **life history** is the pattern of growth, reproduction and survival over an organism's life. Key **life history traits** are age at first reproduction, number and size of offspring per event, number of reproductive events and lifespan.

- **Semelparity** — reproducing once and then dying (Pacific salmon, the male antechinus, a small Australian marsupial whose males die after a short, intense mating season).
- **Iteroparity** — reproducing repeatedly over a lifetime (most mammals and birds).

All organisms have limited energy, so life histories involve **trade-offs**: energy put into reproduction is not available for growth, maintenance or survival, and more offspring means less investment per offspring. Animals may have **direct development** (young resemble small adults) or **indirect development** through a larva that changes form by **metamorphosis**. Larvae often occupy different habitats or eat different food from adults, which reduces competition between generations and aids dispersal.

**Survivorship curves** show the proportion of a cohort surviving to each age. Type I (high survival until old age, as in humans), Type II (constant death rate, as in many birds) and Type III (very high early mortality, as in many fish and marine invertebrates with huge numbers of larvae).

## Worked examples

### Example 1: identifying an unknown animal

A marine animal is described as follows: bilateral symmetry, three germ layers, a true coelom, segmented body with bristles (chaetae), and in its embryo the blastopore becomes the mouth with spiral cleavage.

Step 1 — bilateral and triploblastic: it is a bilaterian, not a sponge or cnidarian.

Step 2 — blastopore becomes the mouth and spiral cleavage: it is a protostome. Spiral cleavage points to Lophotrochozoa.

Step 3 — true coelom, segmentation, chaetae, no exoskeleton or jointed legs: these match phylum Annelida (a polychaete worm), not Arthropoda.

Conclusion: a marine annelid. Note how each feature narrows the options, moving down the branches of the tree.

### Example 2: interpreting a survivorship data set

A researcher follows a cohort of 1000 newly hatched individuals of two species.

| Age (years) | Species X survivors | Species Y survivors |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1000 | 1000 |
| 1 | 50 | 980 |
| 2 | 20 | 960 |
| 5 | 8 | 900 |
| 10 | 3 | 400 |
| 15 | 0 | 0 |

Step 1 — calculate first-year mortality: X loses 950 of 1000 (95%); Y loses 20 (2%).

Step 2 — identify curve type: X has very high early mortality, then a lower death rate, giving Type III. Y has high survival until later life, when deaths increase sharply, giving Type I.

Step 3 — predict life history: X probably produces many small offspring with little parental care (for example a fish releasing many eggs). Y probably produces few offspring with high parental investment.

Step 4 — note: survivorship is usually plotted on a log scale so that a constant death rate appears as a straight line.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking all coelomates are closely related. Body cavity type evolved and was lost more than once.
- Mixing up which opening the blastopore becomes. Protostome means "first mouth": the blastopore becomes the mouth.
- Calling sea stars radially symmetrical animals with radial ancestors. Their larvae are bilateral and they are deuterostomes.
- Assuming diploblastic means "two cells thick". It means two embryonic germ layers.
- Equating semelparity with having few offspring. Semelparous species often produce very many offspring in a single event.

## Exam tips

- Learn the protostome versus deuterostome table; it is often tested in short-answer and multiple-choice form.
- When classifying an animal from features, work in a logical order: tissues, symmetry, germ layers, development, then phylum features.
- Link structure to function: explain why bilateral symmetry is associated with cephalisation and active movement.
- For survivorship data, quote numbers or percentages from the data to justify the curve type.

## Tips to remember

- **"Ecto = exit (outside), Endo = enter (inside), Meso = middle"** (made-up memory trick): ectoderm makes the skin and nervous system, endoderm lines the gut and forms organs like the liver, mesoderm makes muscle, most organs and (in vertebrates) the skeleton and blood. Di-ploblastic = two layers; tri-ploblastic = three.
- **Protostome = "first mouth", deuterostome = "second mouth"**: in protostomes the blastopore becomes the mouth; in deuterostomes it becomes the anus and the mouth forms second. You are a deuterostome, so your first opening was your bottom.
- **Deuterostomes are the "D-R-I-E" group** (made-up memory trick): **D**euterostome cleavage is **R**adial and **I**ndeterminate, the coelom forms by **E**nterocoely (out-pocketing). Protostomes are the opposite: spiral, determinate, schizocoely (splitting). Indeterminate cleavage is why identical twins are possible.
- **Body cavity by the lining**: coelom = fully lined by mesoderm; pseudocoelom = "pseudo" because it is only partly lined by mesoderm (partly endoderm); acoelomate = no cavity at all (flatworms). Remember it is a description, not proof of relatedness.
- **Chordate checklist "Never Do Pigs Talk?"** (made-up memory trick): **N**otochord, **D**orsal hollow nerve cord, **P**haryngeal slits, post-anal **T**ail, at some stage of life.
- **Survivorship curves "I live long, II steady, III die young"** (made-up memory trick): Type I = high survival to old age (humans), Type II = constant death rate (many birds), Type III = very high early deaths (many fish and marine invertebrates).

## Key terms

- **Body plan** — the set of structural and developmental features shared by a group.
- **Cephalisation** — concentration of sense organs and nerve tissue at the anterior end.
- **Germ layers** — embryonic layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm) that form all tissues.
- **Triploblastic** — having three germ layers.
- **Coelom** — a body cavity fully lined by mesoderm-derived tissue.
- **Pseudocoelom** — a body cavity partly lined by mesoderm and partly by endoderm.
- **Blastopore** — the opening of the primitive gut formed during gastrulation.
- **Protostome / deuterostome** — bilaterian lineages in which the blastopore usually becomes the mouth or the anus.
- **Ecdysis** — moulting of a cuticle or exoskeleton.
- **Semelparity / iteroparity** — reproducing once versus repeatedly.

## Summary

- Animal body plans are defined by tissues, symmetry, germ layers, body cavity and development.
- Bilateral symmetry is linked to cephalisation and directed movement.
- Triploblastic animals have mesoderm, from which muscles and many organs form.
- Protostomes and deuterostomes differ in cleavage, coelom formation and the fate of the blastopore.
- Major phyla range from sponges without true tissues to chordates with a notochord and dorsal nerve cord.
- Life history traits reflect trade-offs and can be shown with survivorship curves.

questions.prompt: In a deuterostome embryo, the blastopore usually develops into the:
questions.explanation: Deuterostome means "second mouth": the blastopore becomes the anus and the mouth forms later. A is the protostome pattern, the most common mix-up.

questions.prompt: Which phylum is diploblastic and radially symmetrical?
questions.explanation: Cnidarians have only ectoderm and endoderm and radial symmetry. Echinoderms (B) are tempting because adults look radial, but they are triploblastic deuterostomes with bilateral larvae.

questions.prompt: Why is bilateral symmetry commonly associated with cephalisation?

options.A: Bilateral animals have more germ layers, which are needed to form a brain
options.B: Animals that move in one direction meet the environment first at the front end, so sense organs there are favoured by selection
options.C: Bilateral symmetry prevents sense organs forming on the sides of the body
options.D: Cephalisation is needed to allow a sessile lifestyle

questions.explanation: Directed forward movement means the anterior end first encounters food and danger, so concentrating sensory and nerve tissue there is advantageous. A is tempting because bilaterians are triploblastic, but the link to cephalisation is about movement, not germ layer number.

questions.prompt: A body cavity can act as a hydrostatic skeleton. Which statement best explains how?

options.A: The cavity contains bone-like tissue that muscles pull against
options.B: Fluid in the cavity stores energy for muscle contraction
options.C: Muscles contract against incompressible fluid in the cavity, changing the body's shape and allowing movement
options.D: The cavity keeps organs from moving so the body stays rigid

questions.explanation: Fluid cannot be compressed, so muscle contraction squeezes it and changes body shape, as in earthworm burrowing. D is wrong because a body cavity actually lets organs move independently.

questions.prompt: Early cells separated from a four-cell sea urchin embryo can each develop into a complete larva. This shows that sea urchins have:
questions.explanation: Indeterminate cleavage means early cells' fates are not yet fixed, so each can form a whole embryo. A is the opposite: in determinate cleavage removing a cell leaves the embryo missing parts.

questions.prompt: An animal has bilateral symmetry, a cuticle that it moults, a pseudocoelom, a complete gut and no segmentation. It most likely belongs to:
questions.explanation: A moulted cuticle plus a pseudocoelom and no segmentation fits roundworms. Arthropods (B) also moult, but they are segmented with jointed appendages and an exoskeleton.

questions.prompt: In a cohort of 2000 newly hatched oysters, 1940 die in the first month and the remainder survive for several years with low mortality. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.A: Type I survivorship; high parental care
options.B: Type II survivorship; constant death rate at all ages
options.C: Type III survivorship; 97% early mortality, consistent with many offspring and little parental care
options.D: Type III survivorship; 3% early mortality, consistent with few offspring

questions.explanation: 1940/2000 = 0.97, so 97% die early, the hallmark of Type III, typical of species releasing huge numbers of larvae. D gets the curve type right but inverts the calculation (3% is survival, not mortality).

questions.prompt: Male antechinus die soon after their only breeding season. Which life history interpretation is most accurate?

options.A: They are iteroparous, investing evenly across many seasons
options.B: They are semelparous, putting so much energy into a single reproductive event that survival is sacrificed
options.C: They have a Type I survivorship curve because they all die at the same age
options.D: Their death is a density-independent event unrelated to reproduction

questions.explanation: Semelparity means a single reproductive episode followed by death, reflecting a trade-off of survival for reproduction. C is tempting because deaths are concentrated late, but the key life history point asked about is the single, fatal breeding event.
